q: What's an availability zone?
opts: A physically separate datacenter location within a region, with independent power, cooling, and networking
exp: An availability zone is a physically separate location inside one Azure region — one or more datacenters with independent power, cooling and networking. Spreading VMs across zones protects them from a whole datacenter failing. A paired region is a different region, a rack is a fault domain, and a resource group is just a management container.

q: Can a single availability set span multiple availability zones?
opts: No — availability sets and zones are separate options; choose one per VM
exp: A VM is placed either in an availability set (spread across racks in one datacenter) or in an availability zone (separate datacenters), not both. An availability set doesn't span zones. For zone-level resilience, deploy VMs to different zones or use a zone-spanning scale set.

q: What happens to VMs in the same update domain during planned maintenance?
exp: During planned maintenance, Azure reboots one update domain at a time, so VMs in the same update domain may be rebooted together while the others keep running. They aren't deleted or moved to another region, and they can still be rebooted.

q: An availability set has 2 fault domains and 5 update domains. You deploy 6 VMs. How many VMs share the most-populated update domain?
exp: Azure spreads VMs across update domains round-robin: VMs 1–5 go into update domains 0–4, and VM 6 goes back to update domain 0. So one update domain holds 2 VMs and the others hold 1.

q: Which PowerShell cmdlet creates an availability set?
exp: New-AzAvailabilitySet with -PlatformFaultDomainCount and -PlatformUpdateDomainCount (and -Sku Aligned for managed disks).

q: Which SKU must an availability set use for VMs with managed disks?
exp: Availability sets for VMs with managed disks must use the Aligned SKU, which aligns the disks' storage fault domains with the VMs' fault domains so one storage failure doesn't take down several VMs. Classic is for unmanaged disks, and Premium and Zonal aren't availability set SKUs.

q: A three-tier app needs high availability. What's the recommended pattern for the web tier?
opts: Put web VMs across zones (or in their own availability set) behind a load balancer
Put all tiers in one availability set
exp: Each tier gets its own availability set or zone spread, and traffic is distributed by a load balancer.

q: Which feature co-locates VMs in the same datacenter for the lowest network latency?
exp: A proximity placement group keeps VMs physically close together (in the same datacenter) to get the lowest network latency between them, for example for tightly coupled apps. Availability zones and sets do the opposite: they spread VMs apart for resilience. Dedicated hosts give hardware isolation, not low latency.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: Two VMs in an availability set get a 99.95% SLA
Availability zones are available in every Azure region
A VM in zone 1 and a VM in zone 2 are in different datacenters
An availability set can contain VMs of different sizes
exp: 99.95% for availability sets; not all regions have zones; zones are separate datacenters; sizes can differ within hardware cluster limits.

q: Which CLI command lists the sizes VM1 can be resized to on its current hardware?
exp: list-vm-resize-options shows sizes available on the current cluster; list-sizes shows all region sizes.

q: Which CLI command resizes VM1 to Standard_D4s_v5?
opts: az vm resize -g RG1 -n VM1 --size Standard_D4s_v5
exp: az vm resize --size Standard_D4s_v5 changes a VM's size, which restarts the VM. If the new size isn't on the current hardware cluster, deallocate the VM first. Use az vm list-vm-resize-options to see which sizes are available. The other commands don't exist.

q: Does resizing a running VM cause a restart?
exp: Resizing always restarts a running VM, because it needs different resources from the host. If the new size isn't available on the current hardware cluster, the VM must also be deallocated first so it can move to new hardware. This is the same for Windows and Linux.

q: What's the difference between Stop (from inside the OS) and Stop (deallocate) in the portal?
opts: An OS shutdown keeps the VM allocated and you're still billed for compute; deallocating releases compute and stops compute billing
exp: Shutting down from inside the operating system stops the OS, but the VM stays allocated on its host, so you keep paying for compute. Stopping (deallocating) from the portal or CLI releases the host, which stops compute charges, though you still pay for disks. Neither option deletes disks or the VM.

q: A VM can't be reached via RDP and you suspect host issues. Which action moves it to a new host while keeping its disks?
exp: Redeploy shuts the VM down, moves it to a new host in Azure and starts it again, keeping its disks and configuration. It's the fix for problems caused by the underlying host. Data on the temp disk is lost. Reapply only reapplies configuration on the same host, and resetting the password or resizing doesn't move hosts.

q: You forgot the local admin password of a Windows VM. Quickest fix?
opts: Use 'Reset password' in the portal (VMAccess extension)
Use Bastion to bypass the password
exp: 'Reset password' in the portal (Help → Reset password) uses the VMAccess extension, through the VM agent, to set a new password for the local administrator account without logging in. Recreating the VM is unnecessary, Bastion still needs a valid password, and support isn't needed.

q: You need to run a PowerShell script inside a VM from the portal, with no RDP and no network access to it. Use:
exp: Run Command runs a PowerShell or shell script inside the VM through the VM agent, directly from the portal or CLI, with no RDP, SSH or network access to the VM needed. Bastion still needs RDP or SSH, Network Watcher diagnoses networking, and the serial console is a text console rather than a script runner.

q: A VM won't boot and shows a blue screen. Which features help you see its console output and screenshot?
opts: Boot diagnostics (screenshot and serial log) and Serial Console
exp: Boot diagnostics captures a screenshot of the VM's console and its serial log, so you can see a blue screen or boot error. Serial Console gives interactive access to the VM's console even when networking is broken. The Activity log, Advisor and IP flow verify don't show what's on the VM's screen.

q: VMs in a dev subscription should shut down every evening at 7 PM to save costs. Simplest option?
exp: Each VM has an Auto-shutdown setting that stops (deallocates) it at a set time every day, for example 19:00, and can email you first. That's the simplest way to save costs on dev VMs. Policies, locks and budgets don't shut VMs down.

q: Which service automates OS patching assessment and installation for Azure VMs at scale?
exp: Azure Update Manager checks Windows and Linux machines (in Azure and, via Azure Arc, elsewhere) for missing updates, and installs them on demand or on schedules called maintenance configurations. Advisor gives recommendations, Network Watcher diagnoses networks, and Azure Policy alone doesn't install patches.

q: What does the Azure VM agent do?
opts: Enables VM extensions and handles provisioning and communication with the Azure fabric
exp: The Azure VM agent runs inside the VM and talks to the Azure platform. It handles provisioning (for example setting the admin account) and runs VM extensions such as Custom Script, VMAccess (reset password), Run Command and monitoring agents. It doesn't encrypt disks, back up the VM or act as antivirus.

q: Workloads require physical server isolation for compliance (no other tenants on the host). Which option?
exp: Azure Dedicated Host gives you a whole physical server that runs only your VMs, which meets compliance rules that ban sharing hardware with other customers. Availability sets and proximity placement groups still use shared hosts, and Spot VMs use spare shared capacity.

q: Batch jobs can tolerate interruptions and must be as cheap as possible. Which VM option?
exp: Spot VMs run on Azure's spare capacity at large discounts, but Azure can evict them when it needs the capacity back. That's fine for batch jobs that can restart. Reserved instances need a 1- or 3-year commitment, dedicated hosts cost more, and Premium SSD is a disk type.

q: What eviction policies can Spot VMs have?
exp: When Azure evicts a Spot VM, it either deallocates it (keeping the disks, so you can start it later) or deletes it, depending on the eviction policy you chose. Stop or Restart, Pause or Snapshot and Hibernate aren't Spot eviction policies.

q: A VM needs lower network latency and higher throughput using SR-IOV. Which NIC feature?
exp: Accelerated networking uses SR-IOV so network traffic goes directly between the VM and the network card, bypassing the host's virtual switch. That gives lower latency, less jitter and higher throughput on supported VM sizes. IP forwarding, static IPs and multiple NICs don't improve performance.

q: You want to add a second NIC to an existing VM. What's required?
opts: Deallocate the VM, attach the NIC, and ensure the VM size supports multiple NICs
exp: You can only add or remove network interfaces while the VM is stopped (deallocated), and the VM size must support that many NICs. Add the NIC, then start the VM. You don't need to recreate the VM or add a load balancer.

q: A VM acts as a firewall appliance and must forward traffic not addressed to itself. What do you enable on its NIC?
exp: By default Azure drops traffic arriving at a NIC that isn't addressed to that NIC's IP. Enabling IP forwarding on the NIC lets a firewall or router VM receive and pass on traffic for other addresses (the OS must also be set to forward). Accelerated networking, DNS and static IPs don't change this.

q: Which statement about server-side encryption (SSE) of managed disks is correct?
opts: It's enabled by default with platform-managed keys, and customer-managed keys can be used via a disk encryption set
It must be enabled per disk manually
exp: Server-side encryption (SSE) is always on for managed disks, using platform-managed keys by default. To use your own key, create a disk encryption set that points to a key in Key Vault and assign it to the disks. It covers OS and data disks, needs no manual enabling, and doesn't use BitLocker.

q: Which resource links managed disks to a customer-managed key in Key Vault?
exp: A disk encryption set is the resource that links managed disks to a customer-managed key in Key Vault. You assign it to disks, and it uses a managed identity to reach the key. Encryption scopes are for Blob storage, and a Recovery Services vault is for backup.

q: Before using encryption at host on VMs, what must be done once per subscription?
opts: Register the EncryptionAtHost feature for Microsoft.Compute
exp: Encryption at host must be turned on for the subscription first by registering the EncryptionAtHost feature for the Microsoft.Compute provider. After that you can enable it per VM. Creating a disk encryption set is only needed if you want customer-managed keys.

q: Which Key Vault access setting must be enabled for Azure Disk Encryption?
opts: Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption (enabledForDiskEncryption)
exp: Azure Disk Encryption needs the key vault's 'Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption' access setting (enabledForDiskEncryption) turned on, so the Azure platform can store and read the BitLocker or dm-crypt secrets. Template deployment, purge protection and network settings are separate options.

q: Which CLI command enables Azure Disk Encryption on a VM?
opts: az vm encryption enable -g RG1 -n VM1 --disk-encryption-keyvault kv1
exp: az vm encryption enable turns on Azure Disk Encryption for a VM, with --disk-encryption-keyvault pointing to the vault (and optionally --key-encryption-key for a KEK). It installs the encryption extension, which runs BitLocker or dm-crypt. The other commands don't exist.

q: Which TWO options encrypt the VM temp disk?
opts: Azure Disk Encryption (with the volume type set to All)
exp: Encryption at host and ADE can cover temp disks; SSE alone encrypts managed disks in storage, not the host temp disk.

q: Which CLI command creates a scale set with 2 instances?
opts: az vmss create -g RG1 -n vmss1 --image Ubuntu2204 --instance-count 2
exp: az vmss create creates a virtual machine scale set with the image and starting instance count you give, here 2 (it also creates the network and, by default, a load balancer). az vm create creates single VMs, and the other commands don't exist.

q: Which CLI command manually sets a scale set to 5 instances?
exp: az vmss scale --new-capacity 5 manually sets a scale set to 5 instances. If autoscale is configured, it may change the count again at its next evaluation. The other commands don't exist.

q: Autoscale has a scale-out rule at CPU > 70% and a scale-in rule at CPU < 65%. Instances keep flapping. Best fix?
opts: Widen the gap between thresholds (for example, scale in below 30%) and use cooldown periods
exp: Flapping happens when scaling out pushes CPU just below the scale-in threshold, which removes an instance, which pushes CPU back above the scale-out threshold, and so on. Leave a wide gap between the thresholds (for example out above 70%, in below 30%) and use cooldown periods. Removing the maximum or lowering the minimum doesn't stop it.

q: Traffic peaks every weekday 8 AM–6 PM. How should you scale a VMSS predictably?
exp: An autoscale profile with a recurrence schedule sets the instance count for set times, for example more instances on weekdays from 8:00 to 18:00 and fewer at other times. It scales before the load arrives. Metric rules only react after CPU rises, budgets don't scale, and manual scaling needs someone every morning.

q: What does the Rolling upgrade policy on a scale set do when the model changes?
opts: Updates instances in batches with optional pauses and health checks
Deletes and recreates the scale set
exp: Rolling updates batches; Automatic updates everything immediately; Manual requires you to trigger it.

q: What is the maximum instance count of a scale set using platform images (Uniform)?
exp: Scale sets support up to 1,000 VMs with platform images (600 with custom images in some configurations).

q: Which scale set feature automatically replaces unhealthy instances?
opts: Automatic instance repairs (with an application health extension or LB probe)
exp: Automatic instance repairs watch each instance's health, using the Application Health extension or a load balancer health probe. Instances that stay unhealthy are deleted and recreated automatically. Rolling upgrades change instances in batches, overprovisioning creates extra VMs during scale-out, and Spot is a pricing option.

q: Which scale set setting spreads instances across availability zones?
exp: When you create a scale set, you can specify zones 1, 2 and 3, and Azure spreads the instances across those zones so the set survives a zone failure. Zones can't be added to a scale set afterwards. Fault domain count spreads instances across racks, not zones.

q: Order the autoscale evaluation logic for a scale set:
items: Apply the instance-count change, capped by min/max
Collect the metric over the time window
Compare the aggregated value to the rule threshold
Wait for the cooldown before evaluating again
exp: Autoscale first collects the metric (for example average CPU) over the time window. It compares that value with the rule's threshold. If the rule fires, it changes the instance count but stays within the minimum and maximum. It then waits for the cooldown before evaluating again, so instances can settle.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: Scale sets can be placed behind an Azure Load Balancer
Autoscale can use custom metrics from Application Insights
When scale-out and scale-in rules both trigger, scale-in takes priority
Autoscale can scale based on a storage queue's message count
exp: LB integration and custom metrics are supported; scale-out wins when any scale-out rule fires; queue-based rules are supported.

q: Which service supports moving VMs, NSGs, VNets, and load balancers together across regions with dependency analysis?
exp: Azure Resource Mover moves resources such as VMs, NICs, NSGs, VNets, public IPs and load balancers to another region together. It checks dependencies so related resources move as a group. Azure Migrate is mainly for on-premises workloads, AzCopy copies data, and Export template doesn't move anything.

q: You move VM1 to another subscription. Which dependent resources must be moved together with it?
opts: Its managed disks and network interface (and a VNet if the NIC depends on it)
exp: Dependent resources such as disks and NICs must move with the VM, and the destination subscription must be in the same tenant.

q: VM1 is moved from RG1 to RG2. What happens to its resource ID?
opts: It changes, so scripts referencing the old ID must be updated
The VM gets a new name
exp: A resource ID includes the subscription and resource group, for example /subscriptions/…/resourceGroups/RG1/providers/Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/VM1. After moving to RG2 the ID changes, so update any scripts, templates or alerts that use the old ID. The VM's name and region stay the same.

q: A VM to be moved to another region has Azure Disk Encryption enabled. What do you need to consider?
opts: You need a Key Vault in the target region and must handle the encryption keys and secrets as part of the move
exp: A VM using Azure Disk Encryption needs its keys and secrets in a key vault in the same region as the VM. To move it to another region, you need a key vault in the target region and must copy the encryption keys and secrets there as part of the move. Encrypted VMs can be moved, but encryption isn't removed automatically.

q: A Windows VM should have no public IP but be manageable over RDP from the internet securely. Best option?
opts: Add a public IP with a dynamic address
exp: Azure Bastion lets you RDP or SSH to VMs from the Azure portal over TLS (port 443), without public IPs on the VMs and without opening port 3389 to the internet. Opening 3389 to Any invites brute-force attacks, and a public IP exposes the VM. FTP is unrelated.

q: Which security feature protects VMs against boot-level malware with Secure Boot and vTPM?
exp: Trusted launch turns on Secure Boot (only signed boot components can load), a virtual TPM, and boot integrity monitoring on Generation 2 VMs, protecting them against rootkits and boot-level malware. Encryption at host protects data at rest, accelerated networking speeds up networking, and just-in-time access limits management ports.

q: Which VM generation supports UEFI boot and larger OS disks?
exp: Generation 2 VMs boot with UEFI instead of BIOS, support OS disks larger than 2 TB, and are needed for features such as Trusted launch. Generation 1 uses BIOS. Classic is the old deployment model, not a VM generation.

ctx: VM1: Standard_D2s_v5, in availability set AS1 (3 FDs, 5 UDs), Premium SSD OS disk, Standard SKU public IP, ADE enabled with KV1 in the same region.
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: VM1 can be moved into availability zone 2 by editing its properties
Deallocating VM1 changes its public IP address when it starts again
Resizing VM1 to a size on different hardware may require stopping all VMs in AS1
KV1 could be in a different region than VM1
exp: Zone placement needs recreation; a Standard public IP is static, so it keeps its address after deallocation; resizing within an availability set may require stopping all VMs; the ADE vault must be in the same region.
